presentation: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy
stem:
A 24-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant attends her GP with two days of stinging when she passes urine and a need to go every hour or so. She has no temperature, loin pain or vaginal discharge and is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Advise a high fluid intake and review only if symptoms last beyond one week
options.B: Send a urine culture but withhold antibiotics until the result is available
options.C: Give a urinary alkalinising agent and repeat the dipstick in a week
options.D: Issue a back-up antibiotic prescription to use only if symptoms worsen
options.E: Send a midstream urine culture and start a suitable antibiotic now

correct_answer: E. Send a midstream urine culture and start a suitable antibiotic now
why_correct: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy carries a higher risk of progressing to pyelonephritis, so NICE advises an immediate antibiotic prescription rather than waiting or watchful self-care. A midstream urine sample should be sent for culture before the first dose so that the antibiotic can be reviewed against the sensitivities. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Fluids alone are not enough in pregnancy, where untreated infection can ascend to the kidneys. B. Waiting for the culture leaves her untreated; treatment starts at once and is reviewed when results return. C. Alkalinising agents do not treat the infection and a delayed dipstick adds nothing. D. Back-up prescriptions are used for non-pregnant women; pregnant women should receive an immediate prescription.
pearl: In pregnancy, treat a lower urinary tract infection straight away and send the urine for culture first.
thinking: Pregnant woman with urinary symptoms and no systemic features  ↓  Pregnancy raises the risk of ascending infection  ↓  Immediate antibiotic, not back-up or watchful waiting  ↓  Midstream urine for culture before the first dose, then review against sensitivities
exam_trap: Choosing a back-up prescription or waiting for culture, which suits non-pregnant women or other situations but not pregnancy.
takeaway: A pregnant woman with a lower urinary tract infection needs a culture sample and an antibiotic started immediately.
notes: Re-angled from a vague 'general approach' item to a concrete management choice. Distinct from live PAQ14935 (asymptomatic bacteriuria found at booking) and NEP014/ID054 (pyelonephritis in non-pregnant women). Antibiotic named by class only ('suitable'), no drug/dose recall. Within-batch: PAN259 skipped as repeat of this learning point.
Live duplicate: repeats BX247 (retained placenta as cause of heavy bleeding after birth); also OG013, PAQ16356.
Live duplicate: repeats BX252 (reduced fetal movements: prompt assessment).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman finds a smooth, non-tender swelling about the size of a grape at the lower part of one side of her vaginal entrance. She first noticed it a month ago and it makes cycling slightly uncomfortable. She is afebrile, there is no discharge, and the overlying skin looks normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Epidermal inclusion cyst of the labium

why_correct: A Bartholin cyst is a soft lump on one side near the opening of the vagina, typically at the lower (posterior) part, arising when a gland duct becomes blocked. It is often painless and only becomes tender, hot and red if it turns into an abscess. Source: NHS, Bartholin's cyst (page last reviewed April 2025).
why_wrong: A. A Skene duct cyst lies beside the urethral opening at the front, not at the lower side of the entrance. B. A Gartner duct cyst arises from the lateral vaginal wall, higher up inside the vagina. D. An epidermal inclusion cyst is small and superficial in the skin of the labium. E. A lipoma is a soft, doughy fatty lump and does not follow a gland position.
pearl: The position of a vaginal-entrance cyst points to its origin, and the lower side is the Bartholin gland.
thinking: Painless, non-tender swelling at the vaginal entrance  ↓  Locate it on the vulva: lower side, not beside the urethra and not inside the vagina  ↓  Bartholin gland duct blockage  ↓  Check for signs of infection to exclude an abscess
exam_trap: Confusing a cyst of the Bartholin gland with a Skene or Gartner duct cyst, or calling every vulval lump a malignancy.
takeaway: A painless swelling at the lower side of the vaginal entrance is a Bartholin cyst until proved otherwise.
notes: Source stem was a bare location-to-diagnosis recall; rebuilt as a vignette with plausible vulval and vaginal cyst distractors. Live PAQ16586 is the infected Bartholin abscess (management angle), so not a repeat. NICE CKS Bartholin topic returned 404 on three URLs, so the NHS.uk page was used. Reviewer: the vignette has no red-flag features, so a persistent or atypical lump in an older woman is not tested.
Live duplicate: repeats OG023, OG045, DR072, PAOG015 (abnormal cervical screening result managed through the screening pathway); source key is also a non-specific 'follow the pathway' statement.
Live duplicate: repeats PAQ16147 (folic acid before conception to reduce neural tube defects).

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has had three months of increasing abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a firm pelvic mass. Liver function tests and serum albumin are normal, and an echocardiogram shows no cardiac cause for fluid retention. Ultrasound shows a complex solid and cystic adnexal mass with free fluid in the abdomen.

Which mechanism best explains the free fluid?

options.A: Peritoneal tumour deposits increasing fluid leak and blocking lymphatic drainage
options.B: Raised portal venous pressure caused by underlying fibrosis of the liver
options.C: Heavy loss of albumin through damaged kidney glomeruli, lowering oncotic pressure
options.D: Right-sided heart failure raising systemic venous pressure and fluid transudation
options.E: Thrombosis of the hepatic veins obstructing venous outflow from the liver

correct_answer: A. Peritoneal tumour deposits increasing fluid leak and blocking lymphatic drainage
why_correct: Ovarian cancer spreads within the peritoneal cavity, and tumour deposits on the peritoneal surface increase capillary permeability and obstruct the lymphatics that normally drain fluid, producing malignant ascites. Normal liver tests, normal albumin and a normal echocardiogram argue against the common non-malignant causes. Ascites with a pelvic mass should prompt a suspected cancer pathway referral to gynaecological oncology. Source: NICE CKS, Ovarian cancer (last revised in May 2026).
why_wrong: B. Portal hypertension needs chronic liver disease, and her liver function is normal. C. Nephrotic-range protein loss would show hypoalbuminaemia and oedema elsewhere. D. Heart failure is excluded by the normal echocardiogram. E. Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) causes tender hepatomegaly and abnormal liver tests.
pearl: In ovarian cancer, ascites usually reflects peritoneal disease rather than liver, heart or kidney failure.
thinking: Pelvic mass plus ascites plus bloating  ↓  Exclude liver, cardiac and renal causes with normal tests  ↓  Peritoneal tumour spread with increased leak and impaired lymph drainage  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Assuming all ascites is from portal hypertension and overlooking an ovarian primary in a woman with persistent bloating.
takeaway: Ascites with a pelvic mass in a woman should be treated as ovarian cancer until proved otherwise.
notes: Source asked for a mechanism with absurd distractors (corneal infection etc.); rebuilt with credible alternative ascites mechanisms and normal liver/cardiac/albumin findings so the key is not a restatement. CKS confirms ascites and/or a pelvic mass needs a suspected cancer pathway referral; the peritoneal-seeding mechanism itself is standard pathophysiology teaching, not stated on the CKS page. Live ovarian items (PAQ902, PAAKT141, PMG092) test CA125/CT, not mechanism, so no duplicate.
Live duplicate: repeats OG052 (missed miscarriage diagnosed on scan) and PAQ904; key also hinges on a movable measurement (crown-rump length and absent cardiac activity).
Live duplicate: repeats BX362 (purpose of cervical screening: detect high-risk HPV and precancerous change); also BX961.

stem:
A 31-year-old teaching assistant who is 16 weeks pregnant is told that a child in her class has been diagnosed with slapped cheek syndrome. She sat beside the child for most of a morning two days before the cheeks became red. She feels well and has no rash, joint pain or fever. She telephones her midwife.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure her that no testing is needed because she has no symptoms
options.B: Offer an urgent termination because of the very high fetal risk
options.C: Give oral aciclovir now as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.D: Arrange parvovirus B19 blood tests through the local virology team
options.E: Advise sick leave until delivery and wait to see whether a rash appears

correct_answer: D. Arrange parvovirus B19 blood tests through the local virology team
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis and fetal loss, so a pregnant woman with significant contact should be investigated even if she is asymptomatic. Blood is tested as soon as possible after contact, arranged with the local virology service. Source: NICE CKS, Parvovirus B19 infection (last revised in February 2022).
why_wrong: A. Infection can be asymptomatic yet still harm the fetus, so absence of symptoms does not remove the need for testing. B. Most exposed pregnancies are unaffected, and termination is not an initial response. C. Aciclovir has no activity against parvovirus. E. Waiting for a rash delays diagnosis and a rash may never appear.
pearl: Exposure of a pregnant woman to a child with slapped cheek syndrome warrants early serology, not reassurance.
thinking: Pregnant woman with significant contact to a child with a rash  ↓  Fetal risk exists even when she is symptom free  ↓  Check the immune status and recent infection with blood tests  ↓  Arrange tests through virology and avoid contact with other at-risk people
exam_trap: Reassuring an asymptomatic pregnant contact, or choosing an antiviral that does not work against parvovirus.
takeaway: Test a pregnant woman exposed to parvovirus B19 promptly, because infection can be silent and still affect the fetus.
notes: Source item was a tautology ('why is assessment important': because of fetal complications). Re-angled to the real decision, investigating a pregnant contact; no gestation threshold or time-window recall is keyed. Live PAQ995 (school advice, risk to pregnancy), ID039 and DS099 are different decisions. Contact definition and testing steps taken from the CKS exposure section.
Live duplicate: repeats DS141 (PMOS, unopposed oestrogen, endometrial hyperplasia risk and progestogen protection).
within-batch repeat of PAN6497 (UTI in pregnancy: culture then immediate suitable antibiotic); live PAQ14935 is the asymptomatic bacteriuria variant.
Live duplicate: repeats BX961 and PAQ903 (high-risk HPV result meaning: risk marker, not cancer).
Live duplicate: repeats ID018 (pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox: check varicella IgG, post-exposure aciclovir) and PAAKT180.
Live duplicate: repeats OG016, PAQ905 (hyperemesis with dehydration: IV fluids, antiemetics, assess electrolytes).
Live duplicate: repeats OG043, PAQ16583 (ruptured ectopic with shock) and PAQ1157, OG044 (abruption with shock): resuscitate pregnant woman with bleeding, pain and tachycardia.
Live duplicate: repeats OG026, PAQ907, PAQ14791 (postmenopausal bleeding: suspected cancer pathway referral).
Live duplicate: repeats BX248, BX499, PAQ895, OG006 (severe hypertension with headache/visual disturbance in pregnancy: severe pre-eclampsia, urgent care).
Live duplicate: repeats PAQ919, DF093, DT115 (postmenopausal vaginal dryness and dyspareunia from oestrogen deficiency, vaginal oestrogen).
Live duplicate: repeats OG043, PAQ16583 (ruptured ectopic with shoulder-tip pain and shock: emergency management).

stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 31 weeks of pregnancy reports a sudden gush of clear fluid from her vagina an hour ago, and her underwear has stayed damp since. She has no contractions, abdominal pain or bleeding, and the baby is moving normally. Her temperature and pulse are normal. In the maternity assessment unit the midwife suspects that her membranes have ruptured.

Which initial assessment is most appropriate?

options.A: Nitrazine paper testing of the vaginal fluid as the diagnostic test
options.B: Cardiotocography alone to decide whether the liquor has drained
options.C: Transabdominal ultrasound to measure liquor volume as the only test
options.D: Sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid
options.E: Reassurance that it is probably urine, with routine antenatal review

correct_answer: D. Sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid
why_correct: NICE advises a speculum examination in any woman reporting symptoms suggestive of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, looking for pooling of amniotic fluid. If pooling is seen, no further diagnostic test is needed and care for confirmed rupture, including erythromycin prophylaxis and corticosteroids, is offered. Source: NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. NICE says not to use nitrazine to diagnose membrane rupture because it gives unreliable results. B. A cardiotocograph assesses fetal wellbeing and cannot show whether the membranes have ruptured. C. A reduced liquor volume is not diagnostic and a normal scan does not exclude rupture. E. Dismissing leakage as urine without examination risks missing infection and the chance to start treatment.
pearl: Suspected preterm membrane rupture is confirmed by looking for pooling on speculum examination, not by nitrazine.
thinking: Gush of fluid before 37 weeks with no labour  ↓  Suspect preterm prelabour rupture of membranes  ↓  Speculum examination to look for pooling  ↓  If pooled, treat as ruptured: erythromycin and steroids; if not, use a vaginal fluid biomarker test
exam_trap: Using nitrazine paper or an ultrasound alone to confirm or exclude rupture.
takeaway: Examine with a sterile speculum first when preterm membrane rupture is suspected.
notes: Source was a naming/definition recall (leakage before labour and before 37 weeks = PPROM); that is a bare definition, so re-angled to the initial assessment principle, which is the same condition with a real decision. Live DF055 tests infection assessment in established PPROM and BX253 tests term PROM naming, so not a repeat. Gestation 31 weeks is context only; no gestation cut-off is keyed. I did not cite RCOG GTG 73 (page 404), so no claim about digital examination is made.
